changes: Each day is one idea its exercises share (day 2: a root and its 5th as a power chord, a double stop and a riff), not four unrelated drills.
Each why says what the drill trains and why it works ("a power chord is a root and its 5th, so every chord is a new place for the shape"), so the student could build the next drill.

The same chords come back in new sizes instead of more spider and scale runs: power chords split into notes, double stops inside position 1, G C D as triads (one shape moved, three shapes in one place, a new string set), then a riff that mixes triads, single notes and double stops.
Warm-ups sit where the day's work is (the spider at frets 5 to 8 for position 1, at the 1st fret for the open position), and the spider is on three days, not six.
Tunes come back in a second key with the block's keys ("the notes change, the pattern doesn't"), and day 4's tune is that day's triad played as a melody.
Done is a feel ("until the new chord lands on beat 1 without a gap"), never a count.
Day 7 goes back to day 1's drill at a faster tempo, then asks the student to make up drills by changing one thing, the way every drill this week did.

note: The guitar-beginner week in the new teaching style: each day is one idea, every why says what the drill trains and why it works, and done is a feel. Position 1 returns on six days in new forms, the chords return as power chords, triads and double stops (grip steps in a play-along), tunes move to a second key, and day 7 replays day 1 faster before the student makes up drills.

plan.title: Week 1: position 1, clean changes, triads and double stops
plan.summary: A minor pentatonic position 1, G-C-D changes, and the same chords made smaller: power chords, triads and double stops. One idea a day, each drill says what it trains and why, and by day 7 you make up drills of your own.
plan.progress:
Techniques: the spider is clean from frets 5 and 1 at a slow tempo; double stops are new. Next: the spider in a new finger order, a little faster.
Basic chords: G, C, D and Em change in time at 70 with down strums; the full strum pattern at 80 was only met on day 7. Next: keep the pattern, add a new chord.
Scales: A minor pentatonic position 1 from memory at 80, and phrases that end on the root. E minor in the open position is new. Next: position 2, and joining it to position 1.
CAGED: G, C and D triads on the top strings and one set lower, slowly. Next: the same triads in a second place on the neck.

exercises.title: The spider where position 1 lives
exercises.focus: Frets 5 to 8 · one finger per fret · every string
exercises.why: Position 1 sits at frets 5 to 8, one finger per fret, so warming up right there trains the exact stretch the scale needs.

sections.text: Press Play below to start the metronome and follow the tab: frets 5 to 8 with fingers 1, 2, 3 and 4, one note per beat, on every string and back. The row under the tab shows the finger for each note. Keep going until your hand stays still and only the fingers move.

exercises.title: G, C and D in time
exercises.focus: G-C-D-G changes · down strums at 60 bpm
exercises.why: G, C and D are the 1, 4 and 5 chords of G major, the three chords most songs lean on, so a clean change between them opens up more music than any new chord.

sections.text: The shapes
Tap a chord box to hear the chord, then fret it as shown. Change between two shapes slowly without looking, then look to check that every string rings.
In time

Press Play below to start the metronome; the lit box shows the chord. Strum down on every beat, one bar per chord, and start moving on beat 4. It's working when the new chord lands on beat 1 without a gap.

exercises.title: Position 1, then your own phrases
exercises.focus: A minor pentatonic · position 1 · 60 bpm, the roots, phrases over a band
exercises.why: Every phrase in position 1 sounds finished when it lands on A, so knowing where the three A's are lets you make music from day one.

sections.text: Up and down at 60
Press Play below to start the metronome. Play the position from the low {{1}} up to the high e string and back, one note per beat.
Only the roots
Now only the three {{1}} notes are in play. Hop between them in any order until you can find each one without looking.
Your own phrases
Press Play below to start the band. Make up short phrases from the whole position, leave a gap after each, and end every one on a {{1}}. Then end one on another note and hear how it hangs.

days.theme: Root and 5th: power chords and double stops

exercises.title: Spider, new order
exercises.focus: Frets 5 to 8 · fingers 1, 3, 2, 4 · every string
exercises.why: A new finger order makes each finger move on its own, which is what phrases need once they stop going straight up and down.

sections.text: Press Play below to start the metronome. Same frets as yesterday, but now play frets 5, 7, 6 and 8 with fingers 1, 3, 2 and 4 on every string, up and back. Keep it slow enough that every note rings, until the order stops needing thought.

exercises.title: A5, D5, E5
exercises.focus: Power chords A5-D5-E5 · the shape, in time at 70 bpm, then split into notes
exercises.why: A power chord is a root and its 5th, so once your hand knows the one shape, every chord is just a new place for it.

sections.text: One shape, three places
Tap a chord box to hear it. All three are the same shape, moved to a new string or fret. Strum only the strings with dots, and let the side of your picking hand rest on the others to keep them quiet.
In time
Press Play below to start the metronome; the lit box shows the chord. Strum down on every beat, one bar per chord, until the shape moves without your hand opening up.
Split it

Press Play below to start the play-along. Each bar is the whole chord, two of its notes picked on their own, then the chord again: the tab shows every note. Keep the shape held down the whole bar, so the single notes are already under your fingers.

exercises.title: Double stops in position 1
exercises.focus: A minor pentatonic · position 1 · two notes at once on the B and high e strings
exercises.why: In position 1 the B and high e strings have two notes at the same fret in two places, so the scale you know already holds two double stops, each played with one finger.

sections.text: Press Play below to start the play-along. Each bar goes from one pair to the other: both notes together, two single notes, then the next pair. Follow the tab until the jump between the pairs feels easy.
Now find the two pairs in the position, on the B and high e strings: {{5}} with {{1}}, and {{b7}} with {{b3}}. Make up short lines from the whole position that end on one of the pairs.

exercises.title: A riff of your own
exercises.focus: A minor pentatonic · position 1 · only 1 and 5, over drums and bass in A
exercises.why: A riff is a short phrase repeated, so two notes and a rhythm are all you need to make one up.

sections.text: Press Play below to start the band. Only {{1}} and {{5}} are in play, the two notes of today's power chords. Make up a short riff from them, one at a time or both together, and repeat it until it grooves. Then change one thing: the rhythm, the order or the octave.

exercises.title: G to C, smoother each round
exercises.focus: G-C changes · one-minute rounds
exercises.why: The change you repeat is the one your hand learns, so short rounds on one change grow faster than long ones on many.

sections.text: Tap a chord box to hear it. Change between G and C as smoothly as you can for about a minute, rest, and go again. Each round, try to have the next chord ready a little sooner after the strum.

exercises.title: Position 1 with down-up picking
exercises.focus: A minor pentatonic · position 1 · down-up picking · 70 then 80 bpm
exercises.why: Picking down then up plays two notes with one swing of the hand, so the position can speed up without the hand working harder.

sections.text: Down, up on open strings
Press Play below to start the metronome. Pick each open string down, up, down, up, and follow the arrows under the tab. Keep going until your hand swings evenly, with no stop between the strokes.
Position 1 at 70
Press Play below to start the metronome at 70. Play the position up and down from the low {{1}}, one note per beat, picking down, up all the way.
Position 1 at 80
Press Play below to start the metronome at 80. Same position, same picking. If it feels rushed, go back to 70 for a round.

exercises.title: Call and response
exercises.focus: Position 1 over drums and bass in A · question and answer
exercises.why: A phrase that asks and one that answers is how solos talk, so this turns notes into sentences.

sections.text: Press Play below to start the band. Play a short phrase that ends anywhere (the question), then answer it with one that ends on {{1}}. Keep the answer close to the question, as if replying.

exercises.title: Sol La Sol, in two keys
exercises.focus: A short tune from tab · in G, then in C · 70 bpm
exercises.why: A tune keeps its shape when the key changes, so playing it in two keys teaches your fingers the pattern, not a list of frets.

sections.text: The tune
Press Play below to hear the tune, then play along from the tab. Once you can hum it before you play it, tap C in the Key row below and learn it there. The notes change, the pattern doesn't.

days.theme: Triads: a chord in three notes

exercises.title: G, C and D as triads
exercises.focus: G-C-D-G triads · top three strings · one shape moved, then three shapes · 60 bpm
exercises.why: A triad is the three notes that make a chord, so the same chord can come from one shape slid along the neck or from a new shape right where your hand is.

sections.text: One shape, three chords

Press Play below to start the play-along. One small shape on the top three strings is G, and the same shape further up the neck is C, then D, just as the power chord shape moved on day 2. Strike the three strings on every beat and follow the tab, until the slide lands on beat 1.
Three shapes, one place
Now your hand stays where it is and the shape changes: the same three chords, all within a few frets. Press Play below and follow the tab. Notice which fingers barely move from one chord to the next.

exercises.title: G-Em-C-D strumming
exercises.focus: G-Em-C-D · down strums at 70 bpm
exercises.why: G Em C D is the loop behind countless songs, so a steady strum through it lets you play along with them.

sections.text: The shapes
Tap a chord box to hear it, then fret each one as shown. Go round the loop slowly, until Em to C stops being the slow change.
In time
Press Play below to start the metronome; the lit box shows the chord. Strum down on every beat, one bar per chord.

exercises.title: End on a different note
exercises.focus: Position 1 over drums and bass in A · end on A or on C
exercises.why: The last note sets the mood of a phrase, so choosing it is the first step to sounding like you mean it.

sections.text: Press Play below to start the band. Play phrases that end on {{1}}, then phrases that end on {{b3}}, and listen: the first sounds finished, the second stays open. Then pick the ending each phrase wants.

exercises.title: Do Mi Sol tune, in G, C and D
exercises.focus: A tune on the three notes of a triad · in G, C and D · 70 bpm
exercises.why: This tune uses only the three notes of a triad, one at a time, so your fingers learn today's chords as a melody.

sections.text: The tune

Press Play below to hear the tune and see each note on the neck: it is the G triad, one note at a time. Play along until you can hear the next note before you play it. Then tap C, and then D, in the Key row below. The notes change, the pattern doesn't.

exercises.title: Spider from the 1st fret
exercises.focus: Frets 1 to 4 · one finger per fret · every string
exercises.why: Low on the neck the frets are widest, so the spider there builds the stretch that today's open position needs.

sections.text: Press Play below to start the metronome and follow the tab: frets 1 to 4 with fingers 1, 2, 3 and 4 on every string, up and back. Keep going until the stretch feels as easy as it did at the 5th fret.

exercises.title: E5, G5, A5 riff
exercises.focus: Power chords E5-G5-A5 · down strums at 80 bpm
exercises.why: The power chord shape works on any root, so a riff in E is the same hand you used in A.

sections.text: Tap a chord box to see where each chord sits. It is day 2's shape, in three new places.
Press Play below to start the metronome; the lit box shows the chord. Strum down on every beat, one bar per chord, until the slide from one to the next is smooth.

exercises.title: E minor pentatonic, two places
exercises.focus: E minor pentatonic · the open position, then the 12th fret · 70 bpm
exercises.why: A position's shape doesn't change with the key, it only moves, so the shape you know in A is already E minor pentatonic at the 12th fret.

sections.text: The open position
Press Play below to start the metronome. Play E minor pentatonic in the open position, up and down, one note per beat, starting and ending on {{1}}.
At the 12th fret
The same notes an octave up, in the shape you know from A. With the metronome above still going, play it up and down, then hop between the two positions, landing on a {{1}} each time.

exercises.title: Your A phrases in E
exercises.focus: E minor pentatonic · the open position · over drums and bass in E
exercises.why: A phrase is a shape on the neck, so a phrase you made in A plays in E just by moving it.

sections.text: Press Play below to start the band. Take a phrase you made up in A this week and play it here, then make up new ones that end on {{1}}.

days.theme: A riff from triads, notes and double stops

exercises.title: Triads, one string set lower
exercises.focus: G-C-D-G triads on the D, G and B strings · 60 bpm
exercises.why: Every three neighbouring strings hold the same triads in new shapes, so moving a drill one string set over makes a new drill from chords you know.

sections.text: Press Play below to start the play-along. These are day 4's chords, moved from the top three strings to the D, G and B strings: the shapes change, the chords don't. Strike the three strings on every beat, until each new shape lands on beat 1.

exercises.title: G, C and D without looking
exercises.focus: G-C-D-G changes · down strums at 70 bpm
exercises.why: Looking at your hand is a habit, and a change you can make without looking is one you really own.

sections.text: Press Play below to start the metronome. Strum along, but watch the chord boxes instead of your hand. When a change goes wrong, keep strumming and catch the next one.

exercises.title: A riff: triad, two notes, double stop
exercises.focus: G-C-D-G · triads on the top strings, two notes, a double stop · 60 then 70 bpm
exercises.why: A triad and its single notes are one hand shape, so a riff that mixes them sounds full and never makes your hand jump.

sections.text: G and C at 60

Press Play below to start the play-along. Each bar is the chord's triad, two of its notes picked on their own, then the triad again. Follow the tab, and keep the shape held down so the single notes are already under your fingers.
G, C, D, G at 70
Now D joins, and the last two bars end on a double stop instead of the triad. Once it flows, make it yours: pick two other notes of the chord in the middle of each bar.

exercises.title: A longer tune
exercises.focus: A tune in G · from tab at 65, then on the neck at 75
exercises.why: Reading it once from tab and once from the neck links the numbers to the places your fingers go.

sections.text: From tab at 65
Press Play below to hear the tune and play along from the tab.
On the neck at 75
Press Play below: now the tune is on the neck, a little faster. Play along until you can play it with your eyes closed.

days.theme: Day 1 again, and drills of your own

exercises.title: G-Em-C-D, full pattern
exercises.focus: G-Em-C-D · D . D U . U D U at 80 bpm
exercises.why: This pattern keeps the hand moving down and up on every half beat, so the strums it leaves out are what make the groove.

sections.text: Press Play below to start the metronome. Strum the pattern shown in the boxes on each chord, and keep your hand moving down and up even where it misses the strings. Stay on it until the pattern swings on its own.

tool.pattern: D . D U . U D U

exercises.title: Position 1: day 1 again, then your own drill
exercises.focus: A minor pentatonic · position 1 at 80 bpm · a drill you make up
exercises.why: Every drill this week changed one thing (the key, the tempo, the notes in play), so you can make your own by changing one thing yourself.

sections.text: Press Play below to start the metronome at 80: on day 1 this was 60. Play position 1 up and down from the low {{1}}, and notice what your hands no longer have to think about.

Now make up a drill of your own by changing one thing: the direction, the rhythm, which notes you play, or play it in double stops. Play it until it feels easy, then change another. The same shape in E is below if you want a new key.

exercises.title: Jam over Am and G
exercises.focus: Position 1 over Am-G · land on the root, then on a double stop
exercises.why: Landing on a note of the chord as it changes is the simplest way to make a solo follow the chords.

sections.text: Land on the root
Press Play below to start the backing. Improvise from position 1 and land on the ringed note as each chord comes round: {{1}} for Am.
Land on a double stop
Press Play below to start the same backing. This time end your phrases on one of day 2's double stops on the B and high e strings, and listen for which one suits Am and which suits G.

exercises.title: Your tune, in a new key
exercises.focus: Day 6's tune · in G, then in A · 75 bpm
exercises.why: Playing the week's tune once more, then somewhere new, shows you what has changed in your hands.

sections.text: The tune

Press Play below and play day 6's tune along with it. Then tap A in the Key row below and play it there: the notes change, the pattern doesn't. To finish, play it on your own and change one thing: the speed, the octave or the ending.
